Threshold Scattering for the Three-Dimensional Focusing Energy-Critical Nonlinear Schrödinger EquationThanks: Corresponding author: Dan Han.

Pang-hung Chung Address: Department of Mathematics, Guangdong University of Education, Guangzhou 510640, People’s Republic of China Email address: penghongzhong@yahoo.com and Dan Han Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Louisville, Louisville, Kentucky 40292, USA Email address: dan.han@louisville.edu
Abstract.

Threshold scattering below the ground-state energy and gradient is established for the three-dimensional focusing energy-critical nonlinear Schrödinger equation. A single solution-dependent Gaussian interaction scale, mass-free angular coercivity, and a frequency-gap source estimate control the projected dynamics. These estimates yield quartic spacetime integrability and a zero-mass contradiction, without radial symmetry or an a priori L2L^{2} bound.

Key words and phrases: 
focusing energy-critical nonlinear Schrödinger equation, threshold scattering, interaction Morawetz estimate, concentration compactness, rigidity, nonradial data
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 35Q55; Secondary 35B40, 35P25

1. Introduction

The competition between dispersion and concentration is a central problem in nonlinear Schrödinger dynamics. Linear Schrödinger evolution spreads a wave, whereas a focusing interaction can sustain a stationary profile or produce concentration. At the energy-critical power, rescaling can change the spatial and temporal concentration scales without changing the energy norm. Energy conservation therefore does not by itself distinguish scattering from a persistent concentration scenario. The sharp question is whether the ground state marks the boundary between these behaviors.

In three dimensions this question is particularly delicate for nonradial data in the homogeneous energy space. Such data need not have finite mass, and a concentrated profile may move without any prescribed control of its center. A proof must simultaneously recover positivity for the focusing interaction, accommodate this motion, and control the low-frequency part without assuming the mass that the argument is intended to construct. The present paper gives a Gaussian interaction proof in which these issues are separated into quantitative spatial estimates, a density-selected scale, and an explicit estimate for the projected nonlinear source.

We consider

(1.1) (i∂t+Δ)u=−|u|4u,u(0)=u0∈H˙1(ℝ3),F(z):=|z|4z.(i\partial_{t}+\Delta)u=-|u|^{4}u,\qquad u(0)=u_{0}\in\dot{H}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3}),\qquad F(z):=|z|^{4}z.

The elliptic identity [15] gives 0<A⁡(W)=V⁡(W)0<A(W)=V(W); equality in the Sobolev estimate gives A⁡(W)=G−2​A​(W)3A(W)=G^{-2}A(W)^{3}. Positivity then gives A⁡(W)=GA(W)=G and E⁡(W)=G/3E(W)=G/3.

A strong solution on an interval I∋0I\ni 0 means a function u∈C⁡(I,H˙1​(ℝ3))u\in C(I;\dot{H}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3})) such that u∈Lt,x10​(J×ℝ3)u\in L^{10}_{t,x}(J\times\mathbb{R}^{3}) for every compact interval J⋐IJ\Subset I and such that Duhamel’s formula holds on II. The continuation, stability and scattering criteria used below are those of [3, 26] and [15]. For initial data u0∈H˙1​(ℝ3)u_{0}\in\dot{H}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3}), let u:Imax×ℝ3→ℂu:I_{\max}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{C} denote the unique maximal-lifespan strong solution of (1.1).

With the solution class fixed, the threshold-scattering statement is as follows.

Theorem 1.1.

Let u0∈H˙1​(ℝ3)u_{0}\in\dot{H}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3}) satisfy

E⁡(u0)<E⁡(W),‖∇u0‖2<‖∇W‖2.E(u_{0})<E(W),\qquad\|\nabla u_{0}\|_{2}<\|\nabla W\|_{2}.

Then

Imax=ℝ,‖u‖Lt,x10​(ℝ×ℝ3)<∞.I_{\max}=\mathbb{R},\qquad\|u\|_{L^{10}_{t,x}(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{3})}<\infty.

Moreover, there exist u+,u−∈H˙1​(ℝ3)u_{+},u_{-}\in\dot{H}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3}) such that

limt→+∞‖u⁡(t)−ei​t​Δ​u+‖H˙1=0,limt→−∞‖u⁡(t)−ei​t​Δ​u−‖H˙1=0.\lim_{t\to+\infty}\|u(t)-e^{it\Delta}u_{+}\|_{\dot{H}^{1}}=0,\qquad\lim_{t\to-\infty}\|u(t)-e^{it\Delta}u_{-}\|_{\dot{H}^{1}}=0.

Thus the theorem gives global existence, finite critical spacetime size, and scattering in both time directions in the homogeneous energy class; no L2L^{2} assumption is imposed on u0u_{0}. We next place this statement in the existing scattering theory.

Development of the scattering theory.

For the three-dimensional defocusing energy-critical equation, Colliander, Keel, Staffilani, Takaoka and Tao [6] established scattering for general energy-space data through frequency-localized interaction Morawetz estimates and induction on energy. The difference-variable interaction can follow concentration without choosing a fixed spatial center. For the focusing equation, Kenig and Merle [15] proved the below-ground-state result for radial data in dimensions three through five, using concentration compactness and a rigidity argument. Killip and Visan [17] removed radial symmetry in dimensions at least five through additional decay and negative regularity. Dodson [8] treated dimension four using long-time Strichartz estimates to overcome the logarithmic obstruction. These results identify both the role of the threshold and the sensitivity of the low-frequency argument to dimension.

Recent work on the three-dimensional nonradial problem includes Chung–Han’s conditional rigidity under a center-speed hypothesis [5], and their exclusion of the finite-mass bounded-scale channel [4]. The latter leaves a residual quasi-soliton channel and does not by itself prove scattering for all homogeneous-energy data. Su and Zhao [23] also study this threshold-scattering problem in a recent preprint. Related interaction and moving-scale methods appear in [20, 10, 9, 2].

The homogeneous three-dimensional obstacles.

The threshold inequalities first provide an unweighted coercive gap. Energy conservation, (1.2) and continuity prevent A⁡(u⁡(t))A(u(t)) from reaching GG, since at such a time the energy would be at least G/3G/3. The quantitative energy trap [15] consequently gives

suptA⁡(u⁡(t))≤B2≤(1−γ)​G,A⁡(u⁡(t))−V⁡(u⁡(t))≥(2​γ−γ2)​A​(u⁡(t))\sup_{t}A(u(t))\leq B^{2}\leq(1-\gamma)G,\qquad A(u(t))-V(u(t))\geq(2\gamma-\gamma^{2})A(u(t))

for fixed γ>0\gamma>0. This global inequality does not directly control a focusing interaction with a spatially varying anisotropic Hessian. The negative potential term must be compared with the appropriate directional derivatives at each relative separation.

There is also an infrared obstruction. The energy controls ∇u\nabla u in L2L^{2}, but the sum of low-frequency L2L^{2} contributions can diverge. In particular, even the ground state has infinite mass in dimension three. A Galilean normalization of momentum would introduce a multiple of uu into the gradient and is therefore unavailable without additional control. A fixed-center virial cutoff encounters the separate difficulty that almost periodicity does not furnish a velocity or a sublinear-drift bound for the center. We instead apply a translation-invariant interaction to the finite-mass highpass h=P>ν​uh=P_{>\nu}u. Its mass depends on ν\nu, so recovering positivity by constants involving that mass would not close the argument.

Finally, projection is not compatible with the quintic nonlinearity. The defect P>ν​F​(u)−F⁡(P>ν​u)P_{>\nu}F(u)-F(P_{>\nu}u) contributes both momentum and mass sources. A bound that is merely finite, or that presupposes the desired spacetime norm, cannot be absorbed. The source estimate must use the same quartic quantity and the same terminal intervals as the positive interaction term, with a coefficient tending to zero as ν↓0\nu\downarrow 0.

The spatial estimates and the Gaussian choice.

The first part of our construction converts the scalar threshold gap into a usable two-point tensor inequality. Convex phase reduction expresses the complex-to-modulus difference as an explicit nonnegative square. The angular estimate then treats every nonnegative radial weight for which r​w​(r)rw(r) is bounded and nondecreasing. Its proof combines a one-direction dilation, a two-dimensional inversion, a change of the longitudinal variable, and a normalized incidence-measure identity on great circles. The resulting constant is explicit and independent of the L2L^{2} size. A complementary convolution estimate is obtained through a regularized Fisher-type contraction. The two lemmas have different roles: one controls tangential geometry; the other retains the full convolution quadratic form.

These estimates are combined for a single Gaussian family. Its radial and tangential Hessian components fit the two lemmas, while the density form has a nonnegative Fourier multiplier. Its physical-space kernel changes sign, so the proof keeps the complete quadratic form throughout the core–tail decomposition. The spatial coercivity estimate gives an explicit surviving fraction 77/8177/81 and a strictly positive core contribution on a homogeneous neighborhood of the normalized compact orbit. All cutoff and error choices precede the radius bound, and none depends on the projected total mass.

For a large fixed radius, positivity alone would weaken the quartic control. The density-dependent selector resolves this by choosing the same Gaussian overlap level at every time. Its root is comparable with a⁡(t)=‖h⁡(t)‖44a(t)=\|h(t)\|_{4}^{4}, and the spatial coercivity applies at the normalized radius. More importantly, the Gaussian profile determining the root is also the derivative of the action with respect to radius. The weak continuity equation then gives an implicit identity whose unfavorable part is bounded by a⁡(t)​‖r⁡(t)‖12a(t)\|r(t)\|_{1}^{2}. This is a signed estimate; a small bound on the absolute speed of the radius is not needed.

A spatial frequency-gap estimate and closure.

The projected output is handled by holding the complete density weights fixed and splitting only the solution slot. Exact Fourier-support separation removes every low-weight far interaction. The remaining three terms use the nonendpoint mappings I1:L2→L6I_{1}:L^{2}\to L^{6} and I2:L4/3→L12I_{2}:L^{4/3}\to L^{12}, followed by integer-order highpass estimates. Balancing the near and far losses gives

∫Ij|𝔖k​(𝔬ν,h)|​𝑑t≤Cu​δν​𝔎ν​(Ij),δν:=ν​supt‖P>ν​u​(t)‖2⟶0.\int_{I_{j}}|\mathfrak{S}_{k}(\mathfrak{o}_{\nu},h)|\,dt\leq C_{u}\sqrt{\delta_{\nu}}\,\mathfrak{K}_{\nu}(I_{j}),\qquad\delta_{\nu}:=\nu\sup_{t}\|P_{>\nu}u(t)\|_{2}\longrightarrow 0.

Local endpoint Strichartz remains necessary for the energy-class limit and the final recovery of mass.

We first construct the actual L4L^{4} and L1L^{1} forcing representatives before any time-integrability claim. We then select a cutoff-independent sequence TjT_{j} and control the forcing and its future maximal function by the projected quartic integral. The input cancellation, output frequency gap and signed radius estimate therefore fit one finite-interval absorption. The complete identity is passed to the original weak energy solution while retaining the original, unsmoothed selector. Only after this absorption do we obtain F⁡(u)∈Lt2​Lx1F(u)\in L^{2}_{t}L^{1}_{x}. For each fixed lowpass frequency, dual endpoint Strichartz and no-waste Duhamel construct an actual L2L^{2} value. Mass conservation is invoked after that construction. The time limit is taken first and the frequency limit second, forcing the mass to vanish and excluding the critical element. The ordinary finite-size criterion then supplies both scattering states.

Organization.

Section 2 gives the compactness reduction and interaction structure, Section 3 the forcing comparison, Section 4 coercivity and scale selection, and Section 5 the source estimates, energy-class limiting identity, and rigidity argument.

𝔖kλ​(F⁡(uM)−F⁡(hM),hM)\displaystyle\mathfrak{S}_{k_{\lambda}}(F(u_{M})-F(h_{M}),h_{M}) →𝔖kλ(𝔠ν,h)in L1(I).\displaystyle\to\mathfrak{S}_{k_{\lambda}}(\mathfrak{c}_{\nu},h)\quad\text{in }L^{1}(I).

For the output term,

F⁡(uM)→F⁡(u)in ​Lx1,supM‖F⁡(uM)‖1<∞,F(u_{M})\to F(u)\quad\text{in }L^{1}_{x},\qquad\sup_{M}\|F(u_{M})\|_{1}<\infty,

so

−P≤ν​F​(uM)→𝔬νin ​H1,-P_{\leq\nu}F(u_{M})\to\mathfrak{o}_{\nu}\quad\text{in }H^{1},

and the associated source terms converge in L1​(I)L^{1}(I). For the moving term,

|λ′​𝒥λ​(hM)|\displaystyle|\lambda^{\prime}\mathcal{J}_{\lambda}(h_{M})| ≤(18​A3​B/m)​|λ′|∈L1​(I),\displaystyle\leq(18A^{3}B/m)|\lambda^{\prime}|\in L^{1}(I),
λ′​𝒥λ​(hM)\displaystyle\lambda^{\prime}\mathcal{J}_{\lambda}(h_{M}) →λ′𝒥λ(h)in L1(I).\displaystyle\to\lambda^{\prime}\mathcal{J}_{\lambda}(h)\quad\text{in }L^{1}(I).

Each limit uses dominated convergence and the bounded-kernel pairing representation. For the input limit, (5.2), (5.3) and supM(‖uM‖4+‖uM‖6)<∞\sup_{M}(\|u_{M}\|_{4}+\|u_{M}\|_{6})<\infty give the spatial extension already proved. Together with Step 5, the entire rate converges in L1​(I)L^{1}(I). Both endpoint actions converge by their bounded-kernel L1L^{1} pairings.

7. Identify the original weak source. In L6/5L^{6/5} and 𝒮′\mathcal{S}^{\prime},

E=F⁡(u)−F⁡(h)−P≤ν​F​(u)=𝔠ν+𝔬ν.E=F(u)-F(h)-P_{\leq\nu}F(u)=\mathfrak{c}_{\nu}+\mathfrak{o}_{\nu}.

For a.e. time, (5.9) gives ∇h∈L6\nabla h\in L^{6}. Smoothing that same weak gradient, the L6/5L^{6/5}–L6L^{6} pairings in (5.14) and the classical input identity give

𝔖kλ♭​(E,h)=𝔖kλ​(𝔠ν,h)+𝔖kλ​(𝔬ν,h)=:𝔖kλ​(E,h)a.e.\mathfrak{S}_{k_{\lambda}}^{\flat}(E,h)=\mathfrak{S}_{k_{\lambda}}(\mathfrak{c}_{\nu},h)+\mathfrak{S}_{k_{\lambda}}(\mathfrak{o}_{\nu},h)=:\mathfrak{S}_{k_{\lambda}}(E,h)\quad\text{a.e.}

The output identification uses its actual H1H^{1} realization; the sum is the integrable rate limit. Passing M→∞M\to\infty first on [0,b][0,b] and then subtracting endpoint identities proves, for every s,t≥0s,t\geq 0 in either order,

(5.15) Mkλ⁡(t)​(h⁡(t))−Mkλ⁡(s)​(h⁡(s))=∫st[𝔅kλ⁡(τ)​[h]+𝔖kλ⁡(τ)​(E,h)+λ′​𝒥λ]​𝑑τ.M_{k_{\lambda(t)}}(h(t))-M_{k_{\lambda(s)}}(h(s))=\int_{s}^{t}\bigl[\mathfrak{B}_{k_{\lambda(\tau)}}[h]+\mathfrak{S}_{k_{\lambda(\tau)}}(E,h)+\lambda^{\prime}\mathcal{J}_{\lambda}\bigr]\,d\tau.

5.3. Quartic integrability and the zero-mass contradiction

1. Absorb on the single terminal sequence. For each fixed ν>0\nu>0,

|Mkλ​(h)|≤C​‖h‖23​‖∇h‖2(λ>0),\displaystyle|M_{k_{\lambda}}(h)|\leq C\|h\|_{2}^{3}\|\nabla h\|_{2}\quad(\lambda>0),
Cν:=2​supt≥0|Mkλ⁡(t)​(h⁡(t))|<∞.\displaystyle C_{\nu}:=2\sup_{t\geq 0}|M_{k_{\lambda(t)}}(h(t))|<\infty.

Keep the spatial constants, LL, ϑ\vartheta, and the same Tj,CcmpT_{j},C_{\rm cmp} before decreasing ν\nu. Define

εν:=\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\nu}:= Cin​Ccmp2​(δν+δν2)+Cout​δν+Cmov​(ν2+ν​δν2)⟶0.\displaystyle C_{\rm in}C_{\rm cmp}^{2}(\delta_{\nu}+\delta_{\nu}^{2})+C_{\rm out}\sqrt{\delta_{\nu}}+C_{\rm mov}(\nu^{2}+\nu\delta_{\nu}^{2})\longrightarrow 0.

The constants are independent of j,νj,\nu. Equations (4.20), (5.4), (5.5), the signed moving bound and (5.15) give

cu​𝔎ν​(Ij)≤Cν+εν​𝔎ν​(Ij).c_{u}\mathfrak{K}_{\nu}(I_{j})\leq C_{\nu}+\varepsilon_{\nu}\mathfrak{K}_{\nu}(I_{j}).

Choose ν\nu below all preceding thresholds and so that εν<cu/2\varepsilon_{\nu}<c_{u}/2. Then, for every jj,

𝔎ν​(Ij)≤2​Cν/cu.\mathfrak{K}_{\nu}(I_{j})\leq 2C_{\nu}/c_{u}.

Since Tj↑∞T_{j}\uparrow\infty and the integrand is nonnegative,

𝔎ν​([0,∞))<∞.\mathfrak{K}_{\nu}([0,\infty))<\infty.

Finally,

∫Ij(f2+𝒴2)≤Ccmp2​𝔎ν​(Ij),\int_{I_{j}}(f^{2}+\mathcal{Y}^{2})\leq C_{\rm cmp}^{2}\mathfrak{K}_{\nu}(I_{j}),

so (f,𝒴)∈L2​(0,∞,ℝ2)(f,\mathcal{Y})\in L^{2}(0,\infty;\mathbb{R}^{2}). The last implication is a second monotone-convergence passage with the same comparison witness.

2. Construct a low-frequency L2L^{2} value. Fix K>0K>0 and set QK:=P≤KQ_{K}:=P_{\leq K}. The already used L1→L1L^{1}\to L^{1} and L1→L2L^{1}\to L^{2} bounds give

‖QK​g‖6/5≤‖QK​g‖12/3​‖QK​g‖21/3≤AK​‖g‖1,AK<∞,\displaystyle\|Q_{K}g\|_{6/5}\leq\|Q_{K}g\|_{1}^{2/3}\|Q_{K}g\|_{2}^{1/3}\leq A_{K}\|g\|_{1},\qquad A_{K}<\infty,
𝟏[t,∞)​QK​F​(u)∈Ls2​Lx6/5,‖QK​F​(u)‖L2​([t,∞),L6/5)≤AK​‖f‖L2​(t,∞).\displaystyle\mathbf{1}_{[t,\infty)}Q_{K}F(u)\in L^{2}_{s}L^{6/5}_{x},\qquad\|Q_{K}F(u)\|_{L^{2}([t,\infty);L^{6/5})}\leq A_{K}\|f\|_{L^{2}(t,\infty)}.

The multiplier realizations agree in 𝒮′\mathcal{S}^{\prime}. For this fixed KK, dual endpoint Strichartz [14, 15] constructs

(5.16) mK(t):=−i∫t∞ei⁡(t−s)​ΔQKF(u(s))ds∈L2,‖mK​(t)‖2≤C​AK​‖f‖L2​(t,∞).\begin{gathered}m_{K}(t):=-i\int_{t}^{\infty}e^{i(t-s)\Delta}Q_{K}F(u(s))\,ds\in L^{2},\\ \|m_{K}(t)\|_{2}\leq CA_{K}\|f\|_{L^{2}(t,\infty)}.\end{gathered}

The integral is defined through its dual action on Schwartz tests. Apply the original (2.3) to the same cutoff tests. Commutation gives

QKei​t​Δ=ei​t​ΔQK,QK∂j=∂jQK,\displaystyle Q_{K}e^{it\Delta}=e^{it\Delta}Q_{K},\qquad Q_{K}\partial_{j}=\partial_{j}Q_{K},
∂jmK​(t)=QK​∂ju⁡(t)in ​𝒮′.\displaystyle\partial_{j}m_{K}(t)=Q_{K}\partial_{j}u(t)\quad\text{in }\mathcal{S}^{\prime}.

Sobolev embedding [13] gives

mK​(t)∈L2,∇mK​(t)∈L2,mK​(t)∈H1⊂L6.m_{K}(t)\in L^{2},\quad\nabla m_{K}(t)\in L^{2},\qquad m_{K}(t)\in H^{1}\subset L^{6}.

Finally,

mK​(t)−QK​u​(t)∈L6,∇(mK​(t)−QK​u​(t))=0,\displaystyle m_{K}(t)-Q_{K}u(t)\in L^{6},\qquad\nabla(m_{K}(t)-Q_{K}u(t))=0,
mK​(t)=QK​u​(t).\displaystyle m_{K}(t)=Q_{K}u(t).

The last implication is uniqueness of the L6L^{6} representative with its homogeneous weak derivatives; no additive constant remains.

3. Mass conservation only after construction. The complementary highpass gives

‖(I−QK)​u​(t)‖2≤C​K−1​‖∇u​(t)‖2≤C​B/K.\|(I-Q_{K})u(t)\|_{2}\leq CK^{-1}\|\nabla u(t)\|_{2}\leq CB/K.

At K=1K=1, this and (5.16) imply

u⁡(t)=Q1​u​(t)+(I−Q1)​u​(t)∈L2(t≥0).u(t)=Q_{1}u(t)+(I-Q_{1})u(t)\in L^{2}\qquad(t\geq 0).

Local H1H^{1} theory and homogeneous uniqueness [28] identify the same original solution with the H1H^{1} solution. The mass law and approximation [26] then give

‖u⁡(0)‖2=‖u⁡(t)‖2≤C​AK​‖f‖L2​(t,∞)+C​B/K.\|u(0)\|_{2}=\|u(t)\|_{2}\leq CA_{K}\|f\|_{L^{2}(t,\infty)}+CB/K.

For fixed KK, letting t→∞t\to\infty yields

‖u⁡(0)‖2≤C​B/K.\|u(0)\|_{2}\leq CB/K.

Letting K→∞K\to\infty gives ‖u⁡(0)‖2=0\|u(0)\|_{2}=0, hence u⁡(0)=0u(0)=0 in H˙1\dot{H}^{1} and therefore Ec=0E_{c}=0. This contradicts (2.5). The time limit precedes the frequency limit; no uniform estimate on AKA_{K} as K→∞K\to\infty is needed.

4. Return to the original theorem. Let uu be an arbitrary maximal strong solution with

E⁡(u0)<E⁡(W),‖∇u0‖2<‖∇W‖2.E(u_{0})<E(W),\qquad\|\nabla u_{0}\|_{2}<\|\nabla W\|_{2}.

If Iu≠ℝI_{u}\neq\mathbb{R} or ‖u‖L10​(Iu×ℝ3)=∞\|u\|_{L^{10}(I_{u}\times\mathbb{R}^{3})}=\infty, the critical-element reduction produces an orbit satisfying (2.5), which has just been ruled out. Therefore

Iu=ℝ,‖u‖L10​(ℝ×ℝ3)<∞.I_{u}=\mathbb{R},\qquad\|u\|_{L^{10}(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{3})}<\infty.

Apply the finite-size criterion separately on the two half-lines [15]:

∃u+,u−∈H˙1​(ℝ3),\displaystyle\exists u_{+},u_{-}\in\dot{H}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3}),
limt→+∞‖u⁡(t)−ei​t​Δ​u+‖H˙1=0,\displaystyle\lim_{t\to+\infty}\|u(t)-e^{it\Delta}u_{+}\|_{\dot{H}^{1}}=0,
limt→−∞‖u⁡(t)−ei​t​Δ​u−‖H˙1=0.\displaystyle\lim_{t\to-\infty}\|u(t)-e^{it\Delta}u_{-}\|_{\dot{H}^{1}}=0.

These are the two actual homogeneous gradient-norm limits in Theorem 1.1. This completes the proof of Theorem 1.1.
